title: From Tripods to Bipods Reducing the Queue Number of Planar Graphs Costs Just One Leg

candidates.error_location: Proof of Theorem 3.4 (iterative step), application of Lemma 3.3; together with Definition 3.2 (P2b) and Lemma 3.3
candidates.exact_quote: By Lemma 3.3, we can further assume \( B_{x_{k+1}} \) to induce an acyclic bipod as otherwise we can select a subset of \( B_{x_{k+1}} \) that fulfills this property. In particular, such an acyclic bipod still induces a path that can be extended by \( p_1 \) and \( p_3 \) to obtain a path connecting \( p_1 \) and \( p_3 \).
candidates.claim_content: Setting. G is a plane triangulation with BFS-layering L=(L_0,L_1,...) (L_i = vertices at graph distance i from a root r) and BFS-tree T. Definition 3.2: a subgraph is a 'bipod' if (P1) it has at most 2 vertices in each layer L_i, and (P2) it is the disjoint union of two vertical paths P_1=(u_{s_u},u_{s_u+1},...,u_{t_u}) and P_2=(v_{s_v},...,v_{t_v}) with u_i,v_i in L_i (so the index of a vertex equals its layer), such that if both paths are non-empty then the edge (u_{s_u}, v_{s_v}) belongs to E, i.e. the edge joining the two paths connects their LOWEST-indexed (shallowest, closest-to-root) endpoints. Lemma 3.3 asserts: for a bipod as above there is a non-empty subgraph G' induced by P_1'=(u_i,...,u_{t_u}) and P_2'=(v_j,...,v_{t_v}) with i>=s_u, j>=s_v that is an acyclic bipod; its proof chooses i and then j MAXIMAL with (u_i,v_j) in E, i.e. it deletes the vertices of smallest index (shallowest layers) from both paths. Application in Theorem 3.4: a new bag B_{x_{k+1}} is formed as (P_1 ∪ P_3) \ {p_1,p_3}, where P_1 is the path in T from a vertex t_1 (inside the face) up to its nearest already-assigned ancestor p_1 in bag B_{x_1}, P_3 is the path in T from t_3 up to its nearest assigned ancestor p_3 in B_{x_3}, and (t_1,t_3) is an edge of G. Since p_1 and p_3 are ancestors in a BFS tree, they lie in strictly smaller layers than t_1 and t_3; hence in this bipod the joining edge (t_1,t_3) connects the HIGHEST-indexed endpoints of the two paths, and the lowest-indexed vertices are the children of p_1 and p_3. The paper then asserts the quoted claim.
candidates.suspected_defect: Two linked problems. (i) The bipods actually constructed in Theorem 3.4 have their connecting edge between the deepest (largest-index) endpoints of the two vertical paths, which contradicts Definition 3.2(P2b) requiring the edge (u_{s_u},v_{s_v}) between the shallowest endpoints. (ii) Lemma 3.3 truncates away the SMALLEST-index (shallowest) vertices, i.e. exactly the vertices adjacent to p_1 and p_3. After this truncation the bag is no longer attached to p_1 and p_3, so the quoted claim that 'such an acyclic bipod still induces a path that can be extended by p_1 and p_3 to obtain a path connecting p_1 and p_3' is false, and the subsequent argument that P_1 ∪ P_3 cuts the interior of C_f into two parts (needed for Invariants I3.4.3/I3.4.4) breaks down. The correct lemma for this application would truncate the other end (choose i, j MINIMAL with (u_i,v_j) in E).

candidates.error_location: Proof of Claim 3.5 (inside proof of Theorem 3.4, triangular face case)
candidates.exact_quote: Since the subgraph of G inside cycle Cf is internally triangulated, it follows that there exists a single edge (u′, v′) separating the vertices of V1 from all vertices of different colors, i.e., in particular from Bx₂ and Bx₃. This is only possible if both u′, v′ ∈ Bx₁. But then, Bx₁ is not acyclic, a contradiction to Invariant I3.4.2.
candidates.claim_content: Setting: f=(x_1,x_2,x_3) is a triangular face of a graph H; C_f is a cycle in the plane triangulation G consisting of a path of vertices of bag B_{x_1}, a path of B_{x_2} and a path of B_{x_3}; each bag B_{x_i} induces an acyclic 'bipod' (a connected subgraph that is the union of two vertical paths joined by one edge, hence a tree). Every vertex inside C_f is coloured i if it lies in a subtree of the BFS tree T rooted at a vertex of B_{x_i}; vertices of B_{x_i} are also coloured i. V_1 denotes a non-empty set of unassigned vertices strictly inside C_f coloured 1. The proof assumes for contradiction that no edge inside C_f joins two differently coloured vertices, so every vertex of V_1 has neighbours only in V_1 ∪ B_{x_1}, and then concludes that a SINGLE edge (u',v') separates V_1 from all differently coloured vertices, that u',v' must both be in B_{x_1}, and that this contradicts acyclicity of B_{x_1}.
candidates.suspected_defect: Two gaps. First, a separator of a vertex set inside a triangulated disc need not be a single edge; it is in general a cycle (or a path whose ends are on C_f), so 'a single edge (u',v') separating' is not justified. Second, even if both endpoints u',v' lie in B_{x_1}, the existence of an EDGE with both endpoints in the bipod B_{x_1} does not contradict acyclicity (a bipod is a tree and contains edges); a contradiction would require a CYCLE inside B_{x_1}. The inference 'But then, B_{x_1} is not acyclic' therefore does not follow from the stated premise.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Theorem 3.4, 'Degenerate Step', case analysis of the third triangle vertex t_2
candidates.exact_quote: Because \( P_i \) was chosen to not contain any edge of \( E_{13} \) in its interior and because \( P_i \) is not empty, we conclude that \( t_2 \in V \setminus \{\bigcup_{x \in H} B_x\} \) or if \( i = 1 \) or \( i = p \), we may have that \( t_2 \in B_{x_2} \) or \( t_2 \in B_{x_4} \), respectively.
candidates.claim_content: Setting: f=(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4) is a quadrangular face of H whose associated cycle C_f in the plane triangulation G consists of four paths, one inside each bag B_{x_1},B_{x_2},B_{x_3},B_{x_4}. E_13 is the (non-empty, crossing-free) set of edges drawn inside C_f joining a vertex of B_{x_1} to a vertex of B_{x_3}; these edges partition the interior of C_f into regions P_1,...,P_p with |E_13| = p-1. For a non-empty region P_i (containing at least one vertex not yet assigned to any bag) and an edge e_13 = (t_1,t_3) of E_13 on its boundary, the triangulation of G yields a triangle t=(t_1,t_2,t_3) inside P_i with (t_1,t_3)=e_13. The paper concludes that t_2 is either an unassigned vertex, or (for i=1 or i=p) a vertex of B_{x_2} resp. B_{x_4}.
candidates.suspected_defect: The case t_2 ∈ B_{x_1} (or t_2 ∈ B_{x_3}) is not excluded. If t_2 ∈ B_{x_1}, then (t_2,t_3) is itself an edge of E_13; since P_i has no E_13 edge in its interior, this edge must be another boundary edge of P_i, which is a geometrically possible configuration (the triangle t is then bounded by two E_13 edges). The case analysis therefore appears incomplete, and the subsequent construction (which assigns a new singleton bag joined in H to x_1, x_3 and possibly x_2 or x_4) is not justified in that case.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Theorem 3.4, final paragraph of the 'Degenerate Step'
candidates.exact_quote: If \( i = 1 \) or \( i = k \), it is trivial to see that the newly inserted bipod \( B_y \) is not incident to a vertex from \( B_{x_2} \) or \( B_{x_4} \), respectively, as the triangle into which \( v_y \) was inserted contains no vertex of \( B_{x_2} \) or \( B_{x_4} \).
candidates.claim_content: Setting: in the degenerate step of Theorem 3.4, for a non-empty region P_i inside the cycle C_f of a quadrangular face f=(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4), a triangle t=(t_1,t_2,t_3) with (t_1,t_3) in E_13 is chosen, a new vertex v_y is inserted inside t and joined to t_1,t_2,t_3, and the singleton bag B_y={v_y} is created. Earlier in the same proof it is stated that for i=1 or i=p one may have t_2 ∈ B_{x_2} or t_2 ∈ B_{x_4}, and that in that case the edge (t_2,v_y) splits P_i into two subregions. The quoted sentence then asserts the opposite, namely that the triangle into which v_y was inserted contains no vertex of B_{x_2} or B_{x_4}, hence that B_y is not incident to B_{x_2}/B_{x_4}.
candidates.suspected_defect: Direct contradiction with the earlier case distinction in the same proof: there t_2 is explicitly allowed to lie in B_{x_2} (i=1) or B_{x_4} (i=p), and then v_y IS adjacent to a vertex of B_{x_2}/B_{x_4}. The final argument that every new face f_i satisfies Assumption 3.6 therefore does not cover all cases as written (also note the index 'i = k' where the regions were indexed P_1,...,P_p, so it should be i = p).

candidates.exact_quote: ▶ Theorem 1.5. Let G be a planar graph. Then qn(G) ≤ 38.
candidates.claim_content: The paper proves (Theorem 1.2/1.3) that every planar graph G is a subgraph of K_2 ⊠ P ⊠ H, where P is a path and H is a planar quasi-4-tree, and (Theorem 1.4) that every planar quasi-4-tree H satisfies qn(H) ≤ 6. The standard combination lemma used for such product-structure bounds (the one that yields qn ≤ 49 for planar graphs from K_3 ⊠ P ⊠ H with qn(H) ≤ 5, i.e. 3·3·5 + floor(3·3/2) = 45 + 4 = 49) states qn(H ⊠ P ⊠ K_ℓ) ≤ 3ℓ·qn(H) + floor(3ℓ/2). Substituting ℓ = 2 and qn(H) = 6 gives 3·2·6 + floor(6/2) = 36 + 3 = 39, not 38.
candidates.suspected_defect: The stated constant 38 does not follow from the standard product-to-queue-layout lemma with the paper's own parameters (ℓ=2, qn(H)=6), which yields 39. Either a sharper combination lemma is being used (not visible in the available text) or the arithmetic/constant is off by one.

candidates.exact_quote: Let \( d \) be chosen maximally so that \( L_d \neq \emptyset \) and let \( P = (p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_d) \)
candidates.claim_content: Lemma 3.7 states: if G has an H-partition (H,B) of layered width ℓ with respect to a BFS-layering L = (L_0, L_1, ...), then G is a subgraph of K_ℓ ⊠ P ⊠ H for a path P. The proof lets d be maximal with L_d ≠ ∅ and sets P = (p_1,...,p_d), then argues 'For a fixed layer i ∈ {0,...,d}, K_ℓ ⊠ P contains an ℓ-clique on ((v_1,p_i),x), ((v_2,p_i),x), ..., ((v_ℓ,p_i),x)'.
candidates.suspected_defect: Off-by-one in the index set: the layers used are L_0,...,L_d (d+1 layers), so the path P must have d+1 vertices, but P is defined as (p_1,...,p_d). In particular the vertex p_0 referred to by 'i ∈ {0,...,d}' does not exist in P as defined.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Lemma 4.1 (inductive construction of the layered drawing)
candidates.claim_content: Lemma 4.1 is proved by induction on the number n_f of internal faces of an internally triangulated/quadrangulated outerplane graph G that have been drawn so far. The base case treated is n_f = 1 (a single C_3 or C_4 face containing an outer edge e_o). The inductive step is then introduced by the quoted sentence, i.e. it is assumed that n_f > 2, after which a new face f sharing one edge e_f with the already drawn subgraph G_f is added.
candidates.suspected_defect: The induction skips n_f = 2: the base case covers n_f = 1 and the inductive step assumes n_f > 2, so the case n_f = 2 is not covered. It should read n_f > 1 (equivalently n_f ≥ 2).

candidates.exact_quote: In its canonical embedding, H contains exactly one face, namely f = (x₁, x₂, x₃).
candidates.claim_content: In the initialization of the proof of Theorem 3.4, H is a triangle (x_1,x_2,x_3) drawn with its canonical embedding (the initial C_3 bounding the outer face). The paper asserts that in this embedding H contains exactly one face, namely f = (x_1,x_2,x_3).
candidates.suspected_defect: A plane triangle has two faces, the inner triangular face and the outer face; the statement 'exactly one face' is false unless one restricts to internal faces, which is not stated. Since the iterative step of the proof selects faces f of the canonical embedding of H and reasons about the vertices inside C_f, the distinction between internal and outer faces matters for the invariants (I3.4.3/I3.4.4).

candidates.error_location: Section 2, definition of a vertical path (used for tripods/bipods)
candidates.exact_quote: A vertical path P of t here is a path of G containing exactly one vertex v ∈ Lᵢ of t such that either 1. for all vertices w ∈ P \ {v} with w ∈ Lⱼ, we have i > j, or 2. for all vertices w ∈ P \ {v} with w ∈ Lⱼ, we have i < j.
candidates.claim_content: The paper defines, for a BFS-layering L = (L_0, L_1, ...) of G and a triangle (or edge) t, a 'vertical path' P of t as a path of G that contains exactly one vertex v of t, with v ∈ L_i, such that all other vertices of P lie in layers L_j with j < i (or all in layers with j > i). Later, Definition 3.2 (bipod) requires that the two vertical paths P_1 = (u_{s_u},...,u_{t_u}) and P_2 = (v_{s_v},...,v_{t_v}) satisfy u_i, v_i ∈ L_i, i.e. exactly one vertex per layer.
candidates.suspected_defect: The Section 2 definition of a vertical path does not force one vertex per layer (it only requires all remaining vertices to lie in strictly lower, resp. strictly higher, layers than v), whereas Definition 3.2 implicitly requires exactly one vertex per layer, and the bound 'layered width 2' for a bipod (property P1, |L_i| ≤ 2) depends on this stronger property. The two definitions are inconsistent, and with the weaker Section 2 definition a 'bipod' could contain more than two vertices in a layer.

candidates.exact_quote: Moreover, if there is an edge \( e_2 = (v_{k+1}, v_2) \), where \( v_{k+1} \in B_{x_{k+1}} \) and \( v_2 \in B_{x_3} \), we also connect \( x_{k+1} \) to \( x_2 \). Similarly, if there is an edge \( e_4 = (v_{k+1}, v_2) \), where \( v_{k+1} \in B_{x_{k+1}} \) and \( v_2 \in B_{x_3} \), we also connect \( x_{k+1} \) to \( x_2 \).
candidates.claim_content: Setting: f = (x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4) is a quadrangular face of H; a new bag B_{x_{k+1}} is created from vertical paths ending at vertices t_1 (colour 1, with ancestor p_1 ∈ B_{x_1}) and t_3 (colour 3, ancestor p_3 ∈ B_{x_3}); the new vertex x_{k+1} is joined in H to x_1 and x_3, and additionally to x_2 (resp. x_4) when an edge of G joins B_{x_{k+1}} to B_{x_2} (resp. B_{x_4}). Construction Rule CR2 permits inserting a vertex adjacent to q_1 and q_3 and possibly q_2 and/or q_4 of a quadrangular face (q_1,q_2,q_3,q_4).
candidates.suspected_defect: The two conditions are stated identically: both e_2 and e_4 are defined as edges from B_{x_{k+1}} to a vertex v_2 ∈ B_{x_3}, and in both cases x_{k+1} is connected to x_2. For e_4 the condition must be an edge to a vertex of B_{x_4}, yielding the connection of x_{k+1} to x_4; as written the edge e_4 and its consequence are wrong (wrong bag index and wrong H-neighbour), and the condition for e_2 refers to B_{x_3} instead of B_{x_2}.

candidates.error_location: Proof of Theorem 3.4, Degenerate Step, layer argument for the new vertex v_y
candidates.exact_quote: By Invariant I3.4.5, we have \( t_1 \in L_{i_1}, t_2 \in L_{i_2} \) and \( t_3 \in L_{i_3} \) such that \( i_2 \geq i_3 \) and \( i_2 \geq i_1 \).
candidates.claim_content: Setting: in the degenerate step of Theorem 3.4, t = (t_1,t_2,t_3) is a triangle of the plane triangulation G with (t_1,t_3) an edge of E_13 (t_1 in bag B_{x_1}, t_3 in bag B_{x_3}) and t_2 the third vertex. L = (L_0,L_1,...) is a BFS-layering, so adjacent vertices lie in equal or consecutive layers. Invariant I3.4.5 states that every vertex not yet assigned to a bag is contained in a subtree of the BFS tree T rooted at a vertex of a bag incident to the face containing it. The paper deduces from I3.4.5 that i_2 ≥ i_3 and i_2 ≥ i_1, then assumes w.l.o.g. i_1 ≤ i_3, attaches the newly inserted vertex v_y to t_1 in T (placing v_y in layer L_{i_1+1}), and asserts 'since t is a triangle and t_1 the vertex of t on the lowest layer, we have i_2 − 1, i_3 − 1 ≤ i_1 ≤ i_2, i_3'.
candidates.suspected_defect: There is no justification (and no reason in general) for t_2, the third vertex of the triangle, to lie in the highest layer among t_1,t_2,t_3; Invariant I3.4.5 concerns subtree membership in T, not relative layers. Since t_1 and t_3 are fixed as the endpoints of the E_13 edge, one cannot relabel to make t_2 the highest-layer vertex, so the assumption that t_1 is the lowest-layer vertex of t (used to attach v_y to t_1 and to verify that edges (t_2,v_y) and (t_3,v_y) respect the BFS layering) is unproved and can fail when i_2 < i_1, i_3.

candidates.exact_quote: Since in the \( k \)-th non-degenerate step, at least one vertex of \( v \in V \setminus \{\bigcup_{x\in H} B_x\} \) is assigned to a new bipod \( B_k \), we conclude that our algorithm assigns all vertices in a linear number of iterations and the theorem follows.
candidates.claim_content: The algorithm in the proof of Theorem 3.4 alternates two kinds of iterative steps: non-degenerate steps, each of which assigns at least one previously unassigned vertex of the (augmented) graph to a new bag, and degenerate steps, each of which ADDS new vertices v_y to the graph G (augmenting the triangulation) and creates new singleton bags {v_y} for them. The conclusion asserts that all vertices are assigned in a linear number of iterations.
candidates.suspected_defect: The counting argument only bounds the number of non-degenerate steps by the number of originally unassigned vertices; since degenerate steps create new vertices (which then must themselves be processed and can create new quadrangular faces), the claim of a linear number of iterations (and even termination) does not follow from the stated argument without bounding the total number of vertices created by degenerate steps.
